nameStory: The Ocola Skipper gets its name from the Ocola region of Florida, where this butterfly was first scientifically described. It's also called the long-winged skipper because of its notably elongated forewings compared to other skippers in its family.
description: The Ocola Skipper is a medium-sized butterfly with distinctively long, narrow wings that give it a sleek appearance. With a wingspan of about 1.4 to 1.7 inches, it has a brownish-orange body and wings with subtle markings. This tropical butterfly is actually a rare visitor to New England, straying north from its usual range in the southern United States and Central America. When you spot one, you're seeing a true wanderer that has traveled far from home!

idTips.label: Wing shape
idTips.description: Wings are noticeably long and narrow compared to other skippers, giving it an almost dart-like silhouette when viewed from above

idTips.label: Wing color
idTips.description: Upper wings are tawny orange-brown with darker borders and faint, pale spots that can be hard to see unless the light hits just right

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies with quick, darting movements typical of skippers, but covers more distance with each burst due to its longer wings

idTips.label: Body appearance
idTips.description: Has the thick, robust body typical of skippers, covered in fine hairs that give it a fuzzy appearance when viewed up close

idTips.label: Underwing markings
idTips.description: Underside of wings shows pale yellowish or cream-colored patches that contrast with the darker wing bases

habitat: In New England, Ocola Skippers are extremely rare strays that might appear in open areas like fields, meadows, or gardens, particularly those near wetlands or water sources. When they do show up, it's typically in coastal areas or river valleys where other migrant butterflies tend to appear. Look for them nectaring on flowers in sunny, protected spots during warm weather.

seasonality.spring: Not typically seen in New England during spring months, as any strays would arrive later in the season.
seasonality.summer: The most likely time to spot this rare stray in New England, particularly during warm spells in late summer when southern butterflies sometimes wander north.
seasonality.fall: Occasionally spotted in early fall, but becomes less likely as temperatures cool and any strays either die off or attempt to move south.
seasonality.winter: Cannot survive New England winters and is never observed during this season.

funFact: This butterfly is such a strong flier that individuals have been found over 1,000 miles north of their normal breeding range – imagine a butterfly from Florida showing up in your New England backyard!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other orange-brown skippers, but the Ocola's distinctively long, narrow wings make it stand out. Remember: if the wings look unusually sleek and dart-like for a skipper, and you're in New England, you might have found something really special!
contextualKnowledge: The Ocola Skipper is what butterfly enthusiasts call a "stray" – meaning any individual found in New England has wandered far outside its normal range and cannot establish a breeding population here due to climate limitations.
compareHints: Since there are no other Panoquina species regularly found in New England, compare the Ocola Skipper to other orange-brown skippers like the Delaware Skipper or Least Skipper. The Ocola's wings are significantly longer and more pointed than these relatives, and its overall size is larger. The wing proportions are the key difference – most skippers have relatively rounded, stubby wings compared to the Ocola's sleek profile.
